Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things

Negative Appraisals.value: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
I have permanently changed for the worse
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

vignette: Jamal, a 22‑year‑old African‑American principal at a small suburban school, remembers the first time a photograph of his father’s scarred hands appeared on a dusty kitchen table. The sight of those old photos, a seemingly innocent trigger, snaps his mind back to the night he was beaten, the sting of metal against skin, the echo of his father’s gruff voice. In that moment his mind is flooded with a hard‑to‑recall memory, fragmented pieces of a violent scene that feel more real than any ordinary recollection. The flash of the photo does not simply remind him; it plunges him into the visceral detail of that night, making the past feel all too present. That same image also awakens his negative appraisal of a future he fears: he worries that any sudden confrontation could ignite an uncontrollable rage, that the abuse he endured has permanently altered him, and that bad things will inevitably come to him again. The old photograph thus fuels both the sudden recall of the traumatic event and the mounting sense that he cannot escape the cycle of violence. When Jamal later tries to deliberate on what happened, he finds the memory stubbornly elusive. The fragments that surface are disjointed—his father’s angry face, the sharp crack of a fist, the wet sound of tears—yet they are vivid and disturbingly real. He rationalizes that this inability to fully retrieve the story signals permanent damage, that he has become broken. His fear that he might unleash a similar rage whenever the memory surfaces reinforces his belief that he is helpless against future threats. These negative appraisals, in turn, sharpen the focus on the fragmented recollections, driving Jamal deeper into a spiral where every attempt to remember only brings more fear. The more he thinks about the possibility of being unable to control himself, the more the memory hardens and intensifies, each fragment a sharp reminder that his past is not simply a series of events but a continuous threat. Jamal’s daily routine is punctuated by unpredictable situations that act as triggers. In the school hallway, a sudden commotion—a loud shout, a child tripping—can send him rushing to the sidelines, eyes widening as his mind flips to the chaos of his childhood. These unpredictable moments pull him back into the traumatic memory, where he sees himself as a small, powerless child caught in a world of violence. The suddenness of the trigger not only summons the memory but also activates his negative appraisal: he feels helpless, convinced that any unforeseen event could unleash a fury he cannot control. This loop of trigger, memory, and appraisal intensifies; each unpredictable event becomes a rehearsal of the past, and each rehearsal strengthens his belief that he will inevitably be dragged back into that dangerous scenario. Nightmares compound Jamal’s distress. He often wakes drenched in sweat, his heart pounding, the memory of a father’s hand still clenching his. The residue of these dreams—his abrupt awakening—serves as a trigger that propels him into the memory’s domain. As he struggles to recount the dream’s details, the image of the scarred hand remains vivid, more real than his ordinary memories. The dread that he might one day act violently again, a permanent scar on his future, floods his mind. His negative appraisal of inevitable danger feeds back into the nightmare’s persistence; the more he fears uncontrollable anger, the more the dream resurfaces, each awakening tightening the knot between trigger and fear. In the school environment, Jamal avoids any situation that might resemble those unpredictable moments. He shies away from student council meetings, refuses to address a disruptive class, and even hesitates to sign off on a new curriculum that could lead to unanticipated challenges. His partner, who notices his withdrawal, gently points out how he seems to retreat when plans shift. Jamal, convinced that any shift will trigger the memory and his ensuing rage, declines even the smallest opportunities to engage. This avoidance reinforces his belief in helplessness, and each missed interaction becomes a reminder that he is stuck in a pattern he cannot break. Now, after months of growing isolation and deteriorating relationships, Jamal finally steps into a counseling office. He is haunted by the feeling that his past is a live wire, and the thought that his anger might erupt into something terrible makes him feel trapped. He is most afraid of being seen as dangerous by those he loves, of losing his job and his relationship, and he hopes to find a way to quiet the memory so that the old photos no longer strike him with sudden, painful clarity.
